en: Vimānavatthu: The Mansion of the Man,
Chapter on the Great Chariot (Mahārathavagga)
14. The Mansion of the Great Charioteer “Having mounted this beautiful chariot,
yoked with a thousand horses, which possesses many colors;”
Vāsava, the giver of cities and lord of beings, proceeded step by step along the grounds of the pleasure grove;
both the hubs of his golden chariot wheels—
Exceedingly well-proportioned with shoulders like fruits,
and with well-formed clusters [of hair] established by the Hero among Men,
he shines like the moon on the fifteenth day.
This chariot is covered with a golden net,
adorned with many various jewels;
it has a beautiful sound and a lovely resonance.
And they shine with arms holding chowries.
These navels were fashioned by the mind,
adorning the middle space between the wheels of the chariot.
And these navels are marked with seven circles,
radiant and shimmering like lightning;
this chariot has many-colored coverings.
The Puthu and the Nemi, and the Sahassaraṁsika— their sound is heard like a chorus,
sounding like a fivefold musical ensemble in performance.
In my head, the mind is fashioned like a jeweled crest-ornament—
ever pure, beautiful, and radiant;
it is exceedingly well-adorned with streaks of gold.
The royal beryl shines exceedingly.
And these are the reins fashioned from jewels and moonstones;
the swift, noble steeds are like unto Brahmā.
Great, powerful, and of great speed,
they course through the air just as they know your mind;
and all these together form a group of four.
Knowing your mind, they move exactly as you intend;
carrying you evenly, gentle and unexcited,
these supreme steeds are full of joy.
They shake, they flutter, they fall in the sky,
tossing about their well-fashioned ornaments;
the sound of them is heard like the cry of a bird.
Like the sounding of a fivefold musical ensemble,
there was the rattling of the chariot, the jingling of its ornaments,
and the roar of its wheels as it moved forward with intent to strike.
The sweet sound of the Gandhabba musicians is heard in the various groves of the one who has attained peace;
those women with eyes like the deer’s stand upon their chariots.
With broad, white eyes, smiling and speaking kindly;
draped in nets of beryl, with delicate skin,
they were honored by gods, gandhabbas, and the foremost of heroes.
Clad in garments of deep red and yellow, with wide eyes and lovely glances;
well-born in a noble family, slender-limbed and of pure character.
Standing on the chariot with palms joined in reverence,
they were adorned with shell-like necklaces and armlets, well-dressed,
of beautiful proportions, and possessed of shapely thighs and waists.
With rounded fingers, beautiful faces, and lovely to behold,
they stood upon the chariot with palms joined in reverence.
Others had well-braided hair, while others had their locks hanging loose.
Divided evenly and radiant,
they follow you and delight in your mind;
standing upon the chariot with palms joined, they wait upon you.
Adorned with garlands, their eyes like lotuses and water-lilies,
decorated and scented with the essence of sandalwood—
those women, devoted and delighting in your mind, follow you.
Standing on the chariot with palms joined in reverence,
those women— adorned with garlands of lotuses and lilies, decorated, and scented with the essence of sandalwood— waited upon him.
They, devoted to your mind,
stood upon the chariot with palms joined in reverence;
and those ornaments which were fastened upon your necks—
Illuminating the ten directions in their entirety from her hands, feet, and likewise her head,
she rose up like the autumnal sun.
Shaken by the force of the wind,
the garlands and ornaments upon their arms released a sound that was lovely, pure, and beautiful.
All that is worthy of being heard by the wise:
from the pleasure groves and the two-fold [encampment],
the chariots, the elephants, the musical instruments, and the sound of voices.
They delight you, O Lord of Devas,
just as lutes [resound] with arms like lotus leaves.
Among these many sweet-sounding lutes—
As the Apsarases, highly skilled in dancing upon lotuses, moved with great grace,
they stirred a joy in the hearts of those who beheld their lovely forms.
And when songs and instrumental music, and these dances, come together as one;
then here they dance, and here the nymphs [perform].
Illuminating both groups of women,
he rejoices, awakened by the ensemble of musical instruments,
being honored like Vajirāvudha himself.
Among these many lutes, so sweet and pleasing to the heart,
which deed did you perform for yourself in the past that they stir such joy within your heart?
When you were a human being in a previous birth,
whom did you observe on the Uposatha day?
What practice of the Dhamma or what vow did you find most pleasing?
This is not the result of a small deed performed,
nor of merit previously well-earned through the observance of the Uposatha;
this vast power and majesty of yours is [the fruit of great merit].
That you shine so intensely upon this host of gods—
this is the fruit of your generosity,
or perhaps of your virtue.
"And also regarding the act of joining the palms in reverence— explain that to me when I ask.
That son of the gods was delighted.
Questioned by Moggallāna, he,
being asked the question, explained:
"Of what karma is this the fruit?"
To the one who has conquered the senses, the Buddha whose mind is free from conceit,
the supreme among men, Kassapa, the foremost person,
who opens wide the door to the Deathless—
The God beyond gods, possessing the hundred marks of merit—
I saw him, like an elephant that has crossed the flood,
resembling gold, emerald, and a Bimba fruit.
Having seen him, I was immediately pure-minded;
having seen him whose banner is well-spoken [Dhamma],
whether it be food and drink or even a robe, I gave it to him.
Pure, exquisite, and endowed with excellent flavor—
this I established in my own home for the distribution of flowers,
with a mind free from attachment.
Having satisfied the Supreme among Bipeds with food and drink, with robes,
with hard food, soft food, and refreshments;
Thus, with heaven as my goal, I rejoice in the city of the gods.
Having performed this triple, pure sacrifice that is unbarred by means of this method;
Having abandoned this human aggregation,
like the moon I delight in the city of the gods; there my lifespan,
beauty, happiness, and strength [shall increase].
For the sage who longs for more excellent forms,
abundant and well-prepared food and drink should be set out for one whose mind is free from attachment.
Neither in this world nor in the next is there anyone found who is equal or superior to the Buddha;
he has reached the supreme state of one worthy of offerings.
"For those seeking merit who desire abundant fruits.
The Fourteenth: The Mahāratha Vimāna.
The Fifth Chapter: The Mahāratha Vagga.
Its summary verse:
Maṇḍūka, Revatī, Chatta,
Kakkaṭa, and Dvārapālaka.
"Two duties, two needles,
three elephants, and two chariots:
this is called the first section of men."
The third section for recitation.
